item.title: Assignment 6: Case Studies
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: The case study makes clear from the start that there is no standard model for collaborative practice, and it presents several distinct types. It uses Stravinsky to show how even the same artist can occupy...
item.content:encoded:
The case study makes clear from the start that there is no standard model for collaborative practice, and it presents several distinct types. It uses Stravinsky to show how even the same artist can occupy completely different positions across different projects. For The Firebird in 1910, Stravinsky was the junior party: the scenario was fixed before he arrived, and he was there to write music to fit a structure someone else had already decided. Three years later, on The Rite of Spring, he was the dominant force and Nijinsky had to work around him. At the opposite extreme, Cage and Cunningham built an entire aesthetic philosophy around deliberate non-collaboration during creation: each made their contribution entirely independently, and the two only came together at the moment of performance. Cage’s position was that each art form should support itself without needing the other. Their method was not a failure of collaboration but they genuinely believed that music and dance did not need to serve each other. For them, forcing the two art forms to connect or align would actually diminish both.

Between these extremes sits the Bernstein-Robbins relationship, which is the case study’s main example and the most analytically useful for thinking about my own work. Using Taylor’s framework from the research task, I would describe it as interactive co-operation: there was a clear division of labour (Robbins choreographed, Bernstein composed), but each party had genuine influence over the other’s decisions at the points where their tasks intersected. Bernstein could push back. Robbins could request changes. Neither had total authority over the finished work, even if Robbins held the overall vision. The Oliver Smith dimension adds a third type: Smith, the scenic designer, was simultaneously negotiating with Robbins about what the choreography needed and with the ballet company about what they would finance. His role was closer to consultation, translating between artistic ambition and institutional reality, with decisions being made above and around him.

I recognise myself more in the Firebird situation than in any of these. I came into this project as a student with some compositional training but no experience delivering work for an institution under real constraints. John and Elena had been teaching these students for years and knew what those voices and string players could actually do.

Before this project started I wrote in an earlier log entry that my feelings about collaboration were mixed, and that I thrive on independent work. I predicted that sharing ownership and having to constantly articulate my thought process would feel energy-draining. That prediction was partly right, but not in the way I expected. The part that drained energy was the waiting. Long gaps between emails, decisions that could not be made without institutional sign-off, a performance slot that was possible but not confirmed. The independence I ended up with was not the kind I wanted. I was working alone because communication had slowed, not because I had designed it that way.

This connects to what I found most striking in the Bernstein-Robbins story: the volume of their correspondence. Because both were touring, almost everything happened through letters. Bernstein sent music scene by scene, explained his decisions, and waited for a response. Robbins wrote back with requests or objections. It was slow, but it was continuous. My communication with CAISL has gaps of weeks where I was either waiting or generating material without the back-and-forth that makes iteration meaningful. Bernstein did not send the full score at once and wait for approval.

One thing the case study illuminates that I had not thought about clearly is the role of practical constraints as creative material. Robbins built the characters in Fancy Free around the specific dancers he knew he would have. A character written as a femme fatale in an early draft became more naive once casting was confirmed. The performers’ capabilities shaped the work from inside. I experienced this when Elena told me the 5th grade string students could only play A, B, C#, D, E, F#, and G, forcing me to transpose Part 3 from C minor to B minor. The constraint changed the music. And when she returned after the first reading to say Part 1 had worked but Part 2 would need simplification, that was the same principle: real information about real people making a real piece.

The social dimension of Fancy Free is something the case study handles well and that I initially underestimated in my own work. Robbins built the scenario from direct observation: he noticed that sailors in wartime New York tended to move in threes, and so there are three sailors in the ballet. The social observation preceded and shaped the artistic decision.

My piece has a similar foundation, though I reached it through concept rather than observation. The bridges metaphor is historically specific enough to resist being decorative: the school’s founding was tied to the construction of the Ponte 25 de Abril, and that origin gives the whole structure something real to stand on. But the most socially acute contribution anyone made to the project came from John and Elena, when they proposed the bilingual narration. They understood what it means for a room full of students from different language backgrounds to hear their two languages treated as equal in a single sentence. I had not fully thought that through, and the piece is better because they did.

What I expected from this collaboration was something closer to the Bernstein-Robbins dynamic: a scenario handed to me and a clear brief to respond to musically. What happened was that I wrote the concept, the structure, the narration, the drama, and the music. Part of this was my own instinct toward independent work reasserting itself under pressure. When responses were slow, I filled the gaps with production rather than waiting.

The question the case study makes me think about is whether the Robbins role is compatible with being a student. Robbins had institutional backing, a budget, collaborators with defined contracts, and recognised authority over the project. I am a student with a copywriting background who had never done such a project before. The ambiguity about my actual standing in the collaboration is where most of the difficulties came from, and the case study suggests that resolving that kind of ambiguity early, which Robbins and Bernstein did by defining their respective domains before work began, is not bureaucratic but creative. Clear roles made productive disagreement possible.

What redeemed the final weeks was António Andrade, the drama teacher, who came in late but looked at the script carefully enough to catch a syntactic distinction in the bilingual section I had not considered. He proposed changing “We are the bridges / Nós construímos” to “We are the bridges / Que construímos,” on the grounds that the first version produces two distinct statements while the second links them into one sentence expressed across two languages. He was right, and he had the Portuguese language and literature training to say precisely why. That is the closest the project came to the Bernstein dynamic: someone with genuine expertise in a specific domain pushing back on a specific choice, with a reason, from a position of real engagement. It arrived late. But it arrived, and it changed something. And it came from someone whose role had never been clearly defined at the start, which is itself something to carry forward.

item.title: Research Task 1: Collaboration in Contemporary Music
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: Taylor’s paper argues that “collaboration” is used so loosely in discussions of shared artistic work that it ends up describing almost nothing precisely. He draws a useful distinction between dialogic creation and the specific, different...
item.content:encoded:
Taylor’s paper argues that “collaboration” is used so loosely in discussions of shared artistic work that it ends up describing almost nothing precisely. He draws a useful distinction between dialogic creation and the specific, different thing that happens when people are actually present together, making decisions together. From that distinction he builds a typology of four working relationships: collaboration proper (shared imagination, shared decision-making), two forms of co-operation (divided tasks but mutual influence, either within a pre-agreed framework or interactively), and consultation (one party generates ideas, the other decides). He adds that the closer the language of communication is to the language of the art form itself, the more likely genuine collaboration becomes, which is why jazz musicians can collaborate in ways that composers writing notation generally cannot.

Reading this against my experience with the CAISL piece was uncomfortable in a clarifying way. I had been calling this a collaboration, and I do not think it was, not in Taylor’s sense. The bridges concept, the three-part structure, the musical arc, the full script: I generated all of it and sent it for approval. What came back was enthusiasm, content suggestions, and domain expertise. That maps cleanly onto Taylor’s consultative type, with moments of interactive co-operation when Elena revised the string parts or told me which notes the students could actually play. Those moments changed the music. But they did not change who was imagining the piece.

What strikes me most is that I am not sure the collaboration could have been anything other than consultative, given the conditions. But the deeper issue is institutional. I was engaged as the composer. That role carries assumptions that no amount of goodwill entirely dissolves. What I take from Taylor is not that I should have done this differently, but that I should have been honest about the shape of it from the start, rather than using the word collaboration as a placeholder for something I hoped might develop. Naming the relationship accurately is not a demotion of what John and Elena contributed. It is a more respectful account of what each of us actually did.

item.title: Exercise 2: Work Sharing
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: The piece was conceived for live performance, in CAISL’s main performance space, as part of the 70th anniversary programme. That framing still holds as the intended form, but as of writing this, the live performance...
item.content:encoded:
The piece was conceived for live performance, in CAISL’s main performance space, as part of the 70th anniversary programme. That framing still holds as the intended form, but as of writing this, the live performance is uncertain. Responses from my collaborators have slowed considerably, and the logistical decision (confirmation from the elementary division head, integration of the drama teacher, scheduling) has not fully materialised. I have chosen to continue working regardless, because the piece is worth finishing on its own terms. But this uncertainty has forced me to think differently about what “sharing the work” means.

If the work is ultimately shared only as a score, a set of demos, and a document, it becomes something closer to time-based work in the way a film is time-based: experienced through playback, imagined by a listener rather than witnessed in a space. That is a legitimate outcome, but a different one. The audience encounter I was designing, parents in a room with children performing, becomes hypothetical. I am now writing for an imagined occasion rather than a confirmed one, which changes the energy of the compositional decisions in ways I am still working through.

The beginning has been the most resolved part of the piece from early on, and remains so. The bass and piano opening (a motif that came from my daughter Sofia, who first thought it sounded “scary” and then changed her mind when I added the major piano chords) sets the tone in a way that feels right: something emerging slowly, not announced. The narration enters over this establishing the founding year.

The transitions between sections were a source of productive disagreement with myself. The move from past to present involves a shift from rhythmic, percussive texture to something more melodic and anthem-like. I have been treating it as a slow handover rather than a cut: the strings carry the energy forward while the percussion recedes. The move from present to future is still the hardest. I want it to feel like an opening, not a conclusion, but the modular structure of Part 3 (several 4-bar loops that can be layered and removed by the conductor) makes the transition compositionally tricky. A modular section needs a clear entry point

John’s (choir teacher) contributions in March were mostly about content: historical texts about the Ponte 25 de Abril, the school’s community initiatives, the bilingual dimension. Elena’s (orchestra teacher) contributions have been technical: what the string students can actually play, which notes are accessible, how to revise the arrangement to fit the players. António (drama teacher) has not yet been formally involved. I have been designing the audience encounter largely alone, working from a sense of who will be in that room if a room ever materialises.

item.title: Exercise 1: Exploring Time-based Work
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: Two pieces came to mind. The first was Britten’s Noye’s Fludde, because of how directly it maps onto what I am trying to do at CAISL. It is a community opera for children and amateur performers,...
item.content:encoded:
Two pieces came to mind. The first was Britten’s Noye’s Fludde, because of how directly it maps onto what I am trying to do at CAISL. It is a community opera for children and amateur performers, with professional musicians just sining some parts, built around a single narrative that everyone already knows. What struck me is how Britten uses the congregation hymn Eternal Father, Strong to Save as a structural anchor: the audience sings it, which collapses the distance between watching and participating. The piece exists in time, obviously, but it also exists in a kind of social time, the experience of a community doing something together, publicly, which cannot be repeated in exactly the same form. The staging, the costumes, the spoken word, the music: none of these could be extracted and remain meaningful on their own.

The second piece I spent time with was Christian Marclay’s The Clock (2010), a 24-hour video montage assembled from thousands of film and television clips, each featuring a visible clock or timepiece, synchronised with real time so that the time shown on screen is always the actual time. The piece was shown at the Berardo Collection in Lisbon in 2015, which I was lucky to see at the time. What makes it remarkable as a time-based work is that it refuses any conventional audience relationship. You can walk in at any moment, and the piece will have already been going for hours. You can leave before it ends. There is no beginning you are expected to have witnessed and no ending you are expected to wait for. Marclay described it as a memento mori, and I think that is accurate: the longer you watch, the more aware you become of the time you are spending watching it, which is also the time of your life. The audience’s consciousness of duration becomes part of the work itself.

Thinking about these two pieces clarified something I had been feeling but not quite articulating. Noye’s Fludde works because the audience’s role is defined in advance: they know when they are watching and when they are joining in, and the transition between those states is part of the piece. The Clock works on an entirely different principle: the audience is never anchored to a collective starting point, and the experience varies completely depending on when you arrive. What I have not yet decided, for the CAISL piece, is where our audience sits on that spectrum. Given that the audience will be largely parents and teachers of the children performing, there is a pull toward the congregational model: they will want to feel included in something, not observed from the outside.

I should be honest about one thing Noye’s Fludde also makes me feel: envy at the institutional conditions that made it possible. Britten had a community that was fully mobilised and present. The CAISL piece may end up without a live performance at all. The more I think about Britten’s piece as a model, the more I notice that what I am actually making may be something quite different: a score, a set of intentions, a proposal for something that might one day happen.
